 Tax office breathing down your neck? Here’s how to make it stop

 As of about two weeks ago, the deadline for filing your own tax return has officially passed. Hopefully, you already knew that and this isn’t the first you’re hearing about it, but if not, take this as your reminder that you really need to get around to it.
 For those who’ve employed a tax agent to do it for you, you’re off the hook until May next year. And it turns out that’s not the only reason you have to feel a bit smug.
 Worried you’ve made an improper claim but already submitted your tax return? It’s not too late to amend it. Michael Howard According to Nine , thousands of taxpayers have received letters from the tax office asking them to explain their working out, highlighting deductions (specifically work from home deductions) the ATO thinks they may have gotten wrong.

 What’s the problem?
 This isn’t an uncommon occurrence, with the ATO frequently engaging with taxpayers to clarify and specify details of their self-submitted tax returns.
 “Where claims appear unusual compared with those of taxpayers in similar circumstances, we may contact you before or after your tax return is processed,” an ATO spokesperson said.
 Letters from the ATO are coded in three colours: blue for initial warnings, orange for higher levels of concern, and red for imminent enforcement action.
 Advertisement What you can do about it
 But however colourful they are, getting a letter from the tax office is never a pleasant experience. Here’s what to do if you get one:
 Why are they sent? The ATO sends millions of letters for various reasons every year, and a lot of these are pretty routine, such as BAS notices, super guarantee statements for businesses, and (gentle) reminders if you’ve missed your lodgement for your tax return. But for letters you might get after you’ve already lodged, they’re likely to be because the tax office has identified that your deductions are unusually high when compared to other people in your industry and tax bracket. This is thanks to the ATO’s sophisticated data matching it’s been implementing for a number of years. If you get a letter, it means your claims have attracted the ATO’s attention, but it doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve done anything wrong. It also doesn’t mean you’re getting “audited”, which is a very scary word, so don’t panic, but also, don’t ignore the letter.
 What should you do if you get one? Mark Chapman, head of tax communications at HR Block, says the first thing you should do is identify exactly what the ATO wants you to do. “Carefully read the letter to establish whether it’s simply asking you to review your deductions or whether the ATO is specifically requesting information or a response by a particular date,” he says. “If it’s just a general warning letter, there may be no requirement to respond. However, if the ATO has requested documents or information, taxpayers should comply within the specified timeframe.” Chapman says working out exactly the issue is important as the ATO’s data matching services are not infallible, and often perfectly legitimate claims can be flagged for investigation. If your letter is questioning a deduction you believe is legitimate, you can respond with evidence such as receipts, invoices or bank statements which can allow you to explain your position before they decide. The ATO will then either accept your explanation, or reject it and amend your tax return.
 Can I just ignore it? What did I say like five paragraphs ago? The first letter you get from the ATO (remember the blue, orange, and red system?) is usually just a friendly request for information. However, ignoring it is a great way to have that friendly request upgraded to a full-on audit, or the ATO will just use whatever information it already has to amend your return, which could land you with a far less favourable outcome than if you’d responded. Just because you ignore them doesn’t mean they’ll just forget about you.
 Can you dispute them? If you’re pretty confident what you’ve claimed is legitimate, Chapman says you shouldn’t be afraid to object to the ATO’s amendment. “[Don’t] assume the ATO must be right simply because it’s the tax office. Taxpayers have rights, and if you’ve made a legitimate claim and have the evidence to back it up, you shouldn’t be afraid to challenge it,” he says. You can lodge a formal objection within the objection period, which for most taxpayers is within two years from the original notice of assessment. If the ATO then rejects your objection, you may be able to seek an independent review through the Administrative Review Tribunal or even appeal to the Federal Court.
 How do you avoid getting them? The best way to never get a letter from the ATO is to have a squeaky clean tax record without any improper deductions, which means keeping good records, and never claiming anything that you’re not eligible for. Chapman also notes that if you’ve already submitted your return, but are now just thinking one of your claims might be improper, or you’ve forgotten to declare some income, you can amend your return through MyGov, something he highly recommends doing. “Voluntarily correcting a mistake is usually viewed much more favourably than waiting for the ATO to discover it,” he says.
